extract:
¡Forward, Russia! were a British post-punk revival band formed in Leeds in 2004, active during the mid-to-late 2000s explosion of guitar music emerging from that city. They were part of a fertile scene centred around venues like the Brudenell Social Club and the Cockpit, and around the Dance to the Radio label, which they helped launch alongside contemporaries such as This Et Al and, tangentially, the wider network that included The Pigeon Detectives, iLiKETRAiNS and Sky Larkin. The band's lineup coalesced around vocalist Tom Woodhead, guitarist Whiskas (Rob Canning), bassist Katie Nicholls and drummer Katie Nicholls's bandmate on drums, with Whiskas doubling as a co-founder of Dance to the Radio and a key organiser in the local scene.

Their early releases were built on a jagged, math-inflected post-punk sound indebted to bands like Fugazi, Q and Not U, and At the Drive-In, filtered through the angular energy that dominated British indie in the wake of Bloc Party and Franz Ferdinand. Rather than titling songs conventionally, the band famously numbered them, so their early singles were known simply as Twelve, Nine, Thirteen and Sixteen, a gimmick that drew as much attention as the music itself and reinforced their art-school, systems-driven presentation.

Their debut album Give Me a Wall arrived in 2006 on Mute Records after the initial groundwork on Dance to the Radio, and it collected reworked versions of those numbered singles alongside newer material, delivered in Woodhead's high, shrieking vocal style. The record earned strong reviews in the UK music press, particularly from NME and Drowned in Sound, and the band toured heavily, including festival slots and support tours that put them in front of the Kaiser Chiefs–era Leeds audience. For their second album, Life Processes in 2008, they worked with producer Matt Bayles, best known for his work with Mastodon, Isis and Botch, and the record accordingly took a heavier, more expansive and less frantic direction, trading some of the yelping urgency of the debut for denser, more textured arrangements.

Life Processes received a more mixed reception than its predecessor; some critics admired the ambition and the sonic upgrade, while others missed the wiry immediacy of the singles that had made their name. The band continued to tour but announced their split in 2010, playing farewell shows in Leeds that year. In their relatively brief run they had become emblematic of a specific moment in British indie, when regional scenes built around independent labels and small venues briefly rivalled the London-centric music industry for attention.

After the split, the members dispersed into other projects and industry roles; Whiskas remained involved in Dance to the Radio and Leeds music infrastructure, while Tom Woodhead continued working in music including engineering and mixing work. The band reunited for a tenth-anniversary show for Give Me a Wall in 2016 at the Brudenell Social Club, a one-off that underlined their enduring status as a cult favourite of the era. Their legacy sits with a generation of Leeds bands who proved that a city outside London could sustain a genuinely distinctive scene, and Give Me a Wall in particular is still cited as one of the defining British post-punk revival records of its moment.
title: ¡Forward Russia!
